target.title: LCANet: End-to-End Lipreading with Cascaded Attention-CTC
target.venue: IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG 2018); arXiv v1 2018-03-13

entries.text: LCANet is presented as end-to-end lipreading using visual information alone.
entries.condition: The proposed task is sentence-level lipreading from video frames.

entries.text: GRID is described as 28 hours of video from 34 speakers, each producing 1,000 sentences.
entries.condition: GRID, controlled laboratory recordings.

entries.text: GRID uses a fixed six-word sentence structure, with 51 words and 64,000 possible sentences.
entries.unit: words per sentence; vocabulary words; possible sentences
entries.condition: GRID grammar: command + color + preposition + letter + digit + adverb; sentences are randomly combined.

entries.text: The authors follow prior GRID protocols, randomly splitting sentences into train, validation, and test sets, with 255 test sentences per speaker.
entries.condition: GRID; 34 speakers; random dataset split; the paper does not report the train/validation counts or a speaker-disjoint split.
entries.quote: We follow the evaluation protocol of [3], [5] to randomly divide the dataset into train, validation and test sets, where 255 sentences of each speaker are used for testing.

entries.text: GRID videos are recorded at 25 frames per second, with 75 frames in each three-second sample.
entries.condition: GRID input videos.

entries.text: The mouth-centered input crop is affine transformed to 100×50 using 68 Dlib facial landmarks.
entries.condition: GRID visual input; aligned mouth-region RGB images.

entries.text: RGB mouth images are mean-reduced and normalized; the normalization procedure is not specified.
entries.condition: Input preprocessing; exact mean, scale, channel handling, and whether statistics are train-only are not stated.

entries.text: Training data are augmented using a method similar to LipNet to reduce overfitting.
entries.condition: Training split only; the exact augmentation operations are not stated here.

entries.text: The encoder combines 3D-CNN, highway-network, and bidirectional-GRU components.
entries.condition: LCANet video encoder; the paper describes two stacked highway-network layers.
entries.quote:
The video encoder of LCANet has three components: 3D-
CNN, highway network, and Bidirectional GRU (Bi-GRU).

entries.text: The proposed decoder cascades attention with CTC; the authors claim attention supplies longer context while CTC guides sequential alignment.
entries.condition: Cascaded attention-CTC decoding from encoded video features; no external language-model component is described.
entries.quote:
To capture information ex-
plicitly from longer context, LCANet feeds the encoded
spatiotemperal features into the cascaded attention-CTC
decoder (Figure 4).

entries.text: CTC uses character-symbol labels and models separate character outputs as conditionally independent.
entries.condition: CTC training on character sequences; the paper does not enumerate the complete character vocabulary.

entries.text: Training uses ADAM with initial learning rate 0.0001 and batch size 64.
entries.condition: LCANet trained on GRID in TensorFlow.

entries.text: The model is trained for up to 50 epochs with early stopping; the stopping criterion is not detailed.
entries.condition: GRID; early-stopping metric, patience, and checkpoint-selection rule are not specified.

entries.text: For the joint-loss comparison, λ values from 0.1 to 0.9 were tried and only the best result is reported; the selection split is not identified.
entries.condition: AH-CTC-CE multi-task comparison; it is not stated whether the best λ was selected using validation or test data.
entries.quote: In the experiment, we tried different λ values (from 0.1 to 0.9) and only report the best result here.

entries.text: The authors contrast the single-CTC-loss cascade with a multi-task model trained with weighted CTC and attention cross-entropy losses.
entries.condition: AH-CTC-CE comparator; joint objective is λ·L_ctc + (1−λ)·L_atten.

entries.text: The paper evaluates using CER, WER, and BLEU; lower CER/WER and higher BLEU are treated as better.
entries.condition: GRID sentence-level text predictions; CER/WER use edit distance relative to ground-truth characters/words.

entries.text: The evaluation defines a word as correct only when every character is correct.
entries.condition: Character-level predictions evaluated on GRID; word-level correctness is stated in the results section.

entries.text: The abstract reports 1.3% CER and 3.0% WER on GRID.
entries.condition: GRID; abstract does not specify the test split, speakers, session, seeds, or decoding/LM details; the experiment section describes random splits and 255 test sentences per speaker.
entries.quote: a 1.3 % CER and 3.0 % WER on the GRID corpus database

entries.text: The abstract claims a 12.3% improvement over state-of-the-art methods without naming the metric or comparator underlying that percentage.
entries.condition: GRID; aggregate comparison metric and exact comparator are not specified in the claim.
entries.quote: leading to a 12.3 % improvement compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

entries.text: The main results section reports LCANet at 1.3% CER and 2.9% WER.
entries.condition: GRID; random train/validation/test sentence split; 255 test sentences per each of 34 speakers; fixed six-word grammar, 51-word vocabulary, 64,000 possible sentences; 25-fps, three-second, 75-frame video; character-level cascaded attention-CTC; session partition, seeds/repetitions, and external LM are not reported.

entries.text: Table III reports LipNet at 1.9% CER, 4.8% WER, and 96.0% BLEU.
entries.condition: GRID Table III; random sentence split and 255 test sentences per speaker are the paper's stated protocol; LipNet-specific training, session, seed, and decoding details are not restated.

entries.text: Table III reports LRSW at 3.0 under WER % only (CER and BLEU blank), per the rendered PDF page 7.
entries.condition: GRID Table III; the pypdf text loses the column; pdftotext -layout and the page render place 3.0 under WER

entries.text: The authors state that LRSW was pretrained on the larger Lip Reading Sentences dataset.
entries.condition: LRSW comparator for GRID; its reported external pretraining data are distinct from GRID.
entries.quote: The LRSW model is pre-trained on the large-scale “Lip Reading Sentences” dataset proposed in [5].

entries.text: The AH-CTC-CE ablation reports 2.1% CER, 4.9% WER, and 95.8% BLEU.
entries.condition: GRID Table III; multi-task attention cross-entropy plus CTC; test split as stated for the paper; model-run seeds/repetitions and decoding details are unreported.

entries.text: The H-CTC ablation reports 1.8% CER, 4.3% WER, and 96.4% BLEU.
entries.condition: GRID Table III; highway network without attention; test split as stated for the paper; model-run seeds/repetitions and decoding details are unreported.

entries.text: The A-CTC ablation reports 1.7% CER, 4.1% WER, and 96.7% BLEU.
entries.condition: GRID Table III; attention without highway network; test split as stated for the paper; model-run seeds/repetitions and decoding details are unreported.

entries.text: The full AH-CTC (LCANet) model reports 1.3% CER, 2.9% WER, and 97.4% BLEU.
entries.condition: GRID Table III; random train/validation/test sentence split; 255 test sentences per each of 34 speakers; fixed six-word grammar and 51-word vocabulary; seeds/repetitions, session split, and external LM are not reported.
entries.quote: 6 AH-CTC(LCANet) 1.3 2.9 97.4

entries.text: The authors report 31.6% CER and 37.5% WER improvement over LipNet.
entries.unit: % reported improvement on CER; % reported improvement on WER
entries.condition: GRID, LCANet versus LipNet; test protocol and dataset conditions as above; the paper does not explain the calculation, and Table III WER values are 2.9 and 4.8.
entries.quote: Compared to Lipnet, LCANet has 31.6 % and 37.5 % improvement on CER and WER, receptively.

entries.text: The authors claim the cascaded attention-CTC system outperforms existing methods and the attention-only variant.
entries.condition: GRID comparisons include LipNet, LRSW, and LCANet ablations; reported test protocol is sentence-random rather than explicitly speaker-disjoint.

entries.text: The authors attribute a 0.4% CER and 1.1% WER improvement to the highway network when comparing LCANet with model 5.
entries.unit: % reported improvement on CER; % reported improvement on WER
entries.condition: GRID; LCANet versus model 5 (A-CTC); Table III lists 1.7/4.1 for A-CTC and 1.3/2.9 for LCANet.
entries.quote: Second, the beneﬁt of the highway network is illustrated by comparing LCANet with model {5}, which yields 0.4% improvement on CER and 1.1% improvement on WER.

entries.text: LCANet reaches the stated loss value 4 after 14 training epochs and 20 validation epochs; LipNet takes 38 and 40 epochs, respectively.
entries.value: 14 train; 20 validation; 38 LipNet train; 40 LipNet validation
entries.condition: GRID training and validation losses; target is loss 4; exact checkpoints are annotated in Fig. 6.

entries.text: Figure 6 annotates LCANet train/validation losses as 4.16/4.00 at epochs 14/20 and LipNet losses as 4.27/4.73 at epochs 38/40.
entries.condition: GRID training and validation curves; figure labels include the plotted loss values at the reported epochs.

entries.text: The authors group 43 phonemes into 13 viseme classes, including silence, using the IBM ViaVoice mapping.
entries.condition: GRID confusion-matrix analysis using the cited ViaVoice phoneme-to-viseme mapping.

entries.text: The authors state that cross-viseme misclassification is not statistically significant, but do not identify a statistical test or uncertainty estimate.
entries.condition: Viseme confusion analysis on GRID; the paper provides no test statistic, p-value, confidence interval, or sample-size analysis for this statement.
entries.quote: The misclassiﬁcation between different viseme categories is not statistically signiﬁcant.

entries.text: The authors concede that attention addresses CTC's conditional-independence issue without modifying the loss function itself.
entries.condition: Stated as a limitation and direction for future work.
entries.quote:
LCANet cur-
rently deals with the conditional independence assumption of
CTC using attention mechanisms, but the loss function itself
is not modiﬁed.

entries.text: The authors identify joint audio-visual input as future work; the evaluated LCANet system uses visual information only.
entries.condition: Future extension beyond the visual-only GRID experiments.

entries.text: The paper does not explicitly specify speaker overlap or a speaker-disjoint test protocol; each speaker contributes test sentences after a random dataset split.
entries.condition: GRID has 34 speakers; the paper does not explicitly say whether each speaker also appears in train and validation, so an unseen-speaker evaluation must not be inferred.
entries.quote: We follow the evaluation protocol of [3], [5] to randomly divide the dataset into train, validation and test sets, where 255 sentences of each speaker are used for testing.

entries.text: No random seeds, number of independent runs, or variability/error bars are reported for the headline scores.
entries.condition: GRID training, validation, and test results; the article reports a single set of scores without a repetition protocol.
entries.quote: We train the propose model 50 epochs on GRID with early stopping.

entries.text: The paper does not identify which split selected the best λ or the selected checkpoint; the validation and test set sizes are also not reported.
entries.condition: The article defines random train/validation/test sets and reports best λ from 0.1–0.9, but does not specify the selection data or split counts.
entries.quote: In the experiment, we tried different λ values (from 0.1 to 0.9) and only report the best result here.

entries.text: No chance-level, random, or majority baseline is reported for the fixed-grammar GRID task.
entries.condition: GRID benchmark; performance is compared with selected prior models and ablations, without a chance baseline.

entries.text: No external language model, lexicon, or separate inference-time rescoring aid is described; decoding details beyond attention-CTC are not specified.
entries.condition: GRID results; the paper describes text generation from decoder probabilities but does not document a language-model or lexicon condition.
entries.quote: The CTC decoder generates text predictions from the probability distribution.

entries.text: Session-level partitioning and the number or identity of sessions in the test set are not specified.
entries.condition: GRID test: 255 sentences per speaker under a random dataset split; no session-level split protocol is described.

entries.text: The reported experiments use controlled-lab GRID data; no wild, noisy-environment, or deployed evaluation is reported.
entries.condition: GRID benchmark only in the experiments; the paper's motivations mention broader settings but do not evaluate them.

entries.text: The paper gives no statistical test supporting its statement that cross-viseme confusion is not significant.
entries.condition: Confusion-matrix discussion; no inferential test or uncertainty interval is described.

entries.text: The prose says LCANet beats LRSW on both CER and WER, but LRSW has only a WER (3.0) in Table III and in its source.

entries.condition: GRID Table III; LRSW row: WER 3.0, CER and BLEU blank

entries.text: CTC path alignments can insert blank symbols at arbitrary positions while mapping to the same target sequence.
entries.condition: Character-sequence training with CTC; blank is an alignment symbol.

entries.text: The system outputs text predictions from the decoder's probability distribution.
entries.condition: Character-level lipreading output, decoded from visual video input.

entries.text: Text normalization before CER/WER/BLEU scoring is not specified, including case folding, punctuation handling, and word tokenization.
entries.condition: GRID text predictions and references; only the general CER/WER edit-distance definitions are supplied.

entries.condition: GRID Table III; LRSW row has only one number, placed under CER
entries.quote: However, our method still achieves better CER and WER.

entries.text: The authors call A-CTC (attention + CTC, no highway) the attention-only model.
entries.condition: A-CTC still trains with the CTC loss only (Table II)
entries.quote: In addition, model {5} can be regarded as the attention-only model.

entries.text: The authors explain the multi-task variant's loss by the shared encoder being the only jointly updated part.
entries.quote: The reason is partially because only the shared encoder is jointly updated by both the attention and CTC module in the multi-task model.

entries.text: The authors state the precedent: Hori et al. [43] hybrid CTC/attention with a weighted joint loss; LCANet differs by cascading and avoiding the weight tuning.
entries.condition: stated benefits: no loss-weight tuning; output directly from the softmax
entries.quote: Different from [43], LCANet uses a cascaded attention-CTC decoder.

questions.q: Is the reported test set speaker-independent, and can it be described as unseen-speaker evaluation?
questions.answer: The paper reports a random train/validation/test split and 255 test sentences per speaker, but does not specify a speaker-disjoint protocol. The prior ledger's unseen-speaker characterization is not supported by the paper text.

questions.q: Which WER should a review quote for LCANet: 3.0% or 2.9%?
questions.answer: Both appear in the paper: the abstract gives 3.0% WER, while the main results section and Table III give 2.9%; the discrepancy is not reconciled.

questions.q: What metric and comparison support the stated 12.3% improvement?
questions.answer: The abstract states 12.3% over state-of-the-art methods but does not identify the metric or exact comparator.

questions.q: How reproducible and independently selected are the reported results?
questions.answer: The paper reports no seeds or repeated-run variability and does not identify whether validation or test data selected the best λ/checkpoint.

questions.q: Writer: is the LRSW 3.0 in Table III a CER or a WER in its source?
questions.answer: WER: Chung et al. Table 8 is titled word error rates and gives 3.0% for GRID; no GRID CER is reported there.

questions.q: Writer: does the 37.5% WER improvement over LipNet use 2.9 or 3.0?
questions.answer: (4.8-3.0)/4.8 = 37.5%; (4.8-2.9)/4.8 = 39.6% (reviewer calculation). The stated 37.5% matches the abstract 3.0%.

questions.q: Triage: does Table III put LRSW 3.0 under CER or WER?
questions.answer: WER. pdftotext -layout of PDF page 7 places 3.0 under WER %; the pypdf text had collapsed the columns. Earlier answer (CER) was wrong.
